# 1 Samuel 4 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview and Structure

The chapter records a catastrophic moment in Israel's history: a double defeat by the Philistines, the capture of the ark, and the deaths of Eli, Hophni, Phinehas, and Phinehas' wife. Ellicott calls it "the greatest calamity that had yet happened to Israel" — and notes the whole chapter is "remarkable for the absence of Samuel's name," indicating he was not consulted (Blaikie, cited at preceptaustin.org).

---

## v. 1 — "Thus the word of Samuel came to all Israel …"

**Connection to chapter 3.** The first clause naturally belongs with the end of chapter 3, not chapter 4. "The word of Samuel" is equated with "the word of the LORD" (1 Sam 3:21). The Syriac and Vulgate attach it to the preceding chapter. It means that because Samuel spoke by the word of Jehovah, his word carried binding authority throughout the land — not necessarily that Samuel commanded this particular battle. (preceptaustin.org; Ellicott at biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/4.htm)

**Who started the war?** Ellicott suggests that Samuel may have initially called Israel to arms to throw off Philistine oppression, but this first attempt ended in disaster because Samuel did not yet grasp the depth of moral decay in the nation. Gill notes that some (like Ben Gersom) think Israel acted on their own without consulting the Lord or Samuel, while others think the Philistines were the aggressors: the Hebrew phrase is "went out to meet," implying a defensive response. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/4.htm; Ellicott)

**Ebenezer.** The name means "Stone of Help," but Precept Austin notes it was given by anticipation — the place was only named Ebenezer later when Samuel set up a memorial stone after a victory (1 Sam 7:12). Ironically, at a place whose name means "help," Israel would suffer crushing defeat because they were not relying on God. (preceptaustin.org)

**Aphek.** Located about 5 miles from the Mediterranean coast, at the northeastern edge of Philistine territory. The Philistines were already encroaching on Israelite land. (preceptaustin.org)

**The Philistines.** Enduring Word notes they had Greek military technology — helmets, shields, chain mail, swords, and iron — making them far more formidable than Moab or Ammon. They were organized into five city-states and were "fast reducing Israel to the condition of a subject race" (Smith, cited in Enduring Word). Precept Austin adds that the Philistines appear 288 times in the OT, 182 times in 1-2 Samuel alone. (enduringword.com; preceptaustin.org)

---

## v. 2 — Defeat: about 4,000 Israelites killed

The Philistines drew up in battle array and Israel was "smitten." Gill renders the Hebrew "the battle was spread" (or "diffused"), meaning the battle lines spread across the field — though one Jewish interpretation takes it to mean Israel "forsook" the battle and fled, which was "the beginning of fall or ruin." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/4.htm)

---

## v. 3 — "Why has the LORD brought defeat on us? Let us bring the ark …"

**A right question wrongly answered.** Gill notes the elders were correct to ascribe defeat to the LORD, but "strange" that they were so insensible to the real cause — their own sins, corruption of worship, and idolatry. The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics) says they "assumed … that because they were the acknowledged people of Jehovah they would necessarily receive his help … whether they fulfilled their part of the covenant or not." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/4.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_samuel/4.htm)

**Superstition, not repentance.** Enduring Word (David Guzik) calls this "superstitious manipulation, not humble seeking of God." They wanted to "force God's hand" rather than repent. Spurgeon is quoted: "Instead of attempting to get right with God, these Israelites set about devising superstitious means … They forget the main matter, which is to enthrone God in the life." Ellicott calls it "a curious delusion, this baseless hope of the elders, that the unseen God was inseparably connected with that strange and beautiful symbol of His presence." (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/4.htm)

**Precedent.** The ark had gone into battle before — at Jericho (Josh 6:6-8), against the Midianites (Num 31:6), and later with Saul and David — but in those cases it was God's command, not human superstition. (enduringword.com)

**Providential overruling.** Gill observes that God overruled this foolish decision to bring Hophni and Phinehas into the camp "that they might be slain in one day, according to the divine prediction" (1 Sam 2:34). (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/4.htm)

---

## v. 4 — The ark brought from Shiloh; Hophni and Phinehas accompany it

**"The LORD of Hosts, who sits enthroned between the cherubim."** This full title emphasizes the irony: they acknowledge God's majesty yet treat His throne as a talisman. Ellicott notes the bitter contrast the writer sets up — the glorious throne of God escorted by wicked, abandoned priests. Gill adds that Hophni and Phinehas either took the ark without Eli's leave or attended it as it was carried by other priests/Levites. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/4.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/4.htm)

---

## v. 5 — The great shout that shook the ground

Ellicott observes this was likely the first time the ark had been brought from the permanent sanctuary at Shiloh into a military camp since the conquest of Canaan. The shout expressed false confidence. Enduring Word quotes Spurgeon: "Do not be so foolish as to suppose that because there is loud noise there must also be faith. Faith is a still water, it flows deep." Adam Clarke (cited by Guzik): "Had they humbled themselves, and prayed devoutly … they would have been heard and saved. Their shouting proved both their vanity and irreligion." (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/4.htm)

---

## vv. 6–7 — The Philistines' fear

The Philistines recognized the ark represented the presence of God. Ellicott says both sides were "equally superstitious" — both thought deity was connected to the lifeless gold and wood. The Philistines had some excuse: they knew the tradition of the ark leading Israel to victory under Joshua. They cried, "God has come into the camp!" and "nothing like this has happened before" — meaning the ark had not been brought into battle like this in their experience. (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/4.htm)

---

## v. 8 — "These mighty gods … who struck the Egyptians with all kinds of plagues in the wilderness"

**Polytheistic language.** Ellicott notes the Philistines use the plural "mighty gods" (Elohim addirim), reflecting their polytheistic worldview — they had no concept of the one true God. Their fear was based on Egyptian traditions: they knew the God of Israel had devastated Egypt. Gill notes the apparent historical inaccuracy (plagues "in the wilderness" rather than in Egypt), but says this is understandable from pagans with only vague knowledge of Israel's history; some commentators suggest the reference is to the destruction of Pharaoh's army at the Red Sea, which had wilderness on both sides. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/4.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/4.htm)

---

## v. 9 — "Take courage and be men, O Philistines! … be men and fight!"

The Philistines chose to resist rather than submit. Enduring Word notes: "If they really believed their gods were greater … they should not have been worried. If they believed the God of Israel was greater … they should have submitted." Instead they fought with the courage of desperate men. Ellicott observes that Paul may have had this rallying cry in mind when he wrote "Quit ye like men; be strong" (1 Cor 16:13). (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/4.htm)

---

## vv. 10–11 — The catastrophic defeat: 30,000 dead, ark captured, Hophni and Phinehas killed

**Worse with the ark than without it.** With the ark, Israel lost 30,000 — more than seven times the 4,000 lost in the first battle. God would not be coerced by superstition. Enduring Word: "God is a person, not a genie to be summoned at the will of man." (enduringword.com)

**Three reasons for the defeat** (per Enduring Word): (1) The Philistines fought with desperate courage; (2) Israelites thought the battle would be easy and didn't try as hard; (3) God did not bless superstition. (enduringword.com)

**The ark captured.** Ellicott states the bare fact without comment, calling it "the greatest calamity that had yet happened to Israel." But the capture taught an eternal truth: "the living God does not bind His presence to a dead thing" (Erdmann, cited in Ellicott). Bishop Wordsworth adds: "that ark was taken by idolaters" — the very ark made at Sinai, before which Jordan fled and Jericho fell. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/4.htm)

**Extra-biblical reference.** Enduring Word notes that in the late 1970s, a five-line inscription was found on a grain silo at Izbet Sarteh containing a Philistine account of this battle, mentioning the priest Hophni by name — the earliest known extra-biblical reference to an Old Testament event. (enduringword.com)

**Fulfilled prophecy.** The deaths of Hophni and Phinehas on the same day fulfilled the prophecy of the man of God in 1 Samuel 2:34. Gill cites Josephus' tradition that the brothers had been charged by Eli that if the ark were taken, they should not desire to live or dare return to him. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/4.htm)

---

## v. 12 — The Benjamite messenger: torn clothes and dirt on his head

The torn clothes and dirt were traditional signs of mourning, signaling bad news before a word was spoken. A rabbinic tradition (noted by Gill and Enduring Word) identifies this messenger as Saul, but both sources call this unfounded. The battle site Aphek was at least 20 miles from Shiloh, mostly uphill. (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/4.htm)

---

## vv. 13–14 — Eli waiting; the city cries out

Eli sat by the road, watching (or at the gate, per the LXX), "for his heart trembled for the ark of God." Ellicott notes that Eli's heart trembled particularly for the ark because he knew he had let it go on an unwise, superstitious errand against his better judgment. He "knew too much of the Eternal Guardian of Israel to put any real trust in the power of the lifeless Ark." The text says Eli was sitting at a place the Hebrew calls "the hand of the way" — possibly where two roads met, marked by a directional sign. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/4.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/4.htm)

---

## v. 15 — Eli: 98 years old, blind

The Hebrew says his eyes "stood" — fixed, immovable, a description of "black cataract (amaurosis), which not infrequently occurs at a very great age from paralysis of the optic nerves" (Keil, cited in Ellicott). The LXX reads "ninety" years and the Syriac "seventy-eight," illustrating the textual variations common with numbers in Hebrew manuscripts, which used letters to represent numerals. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/4.htm)

---

## vv. 16–17 — The messenger's report

The messenger identifies himself as having fled the battle that very day. His report comes in escalating stages: (1) Israel fled; (2) great slaughter; (3) your two sons are dead; (4) the ark of God has been captured. Gill notes this structured delivery, with the worst news last. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/4.htm)

---

## v. 18 — Eli's death

**At the mention of the ark, not his sons.** The text is precise: "when he made mention of the ark of God, Eli fell." John Trapp (cited in Enduring Word): "No sword of a Philistine could have slain him any more powerfully; neither can you say whether his neck or his heart were broken first." This reveals Eli's true priority: the ark of God mattered more to him than his own sons. Ellicott says the chronicler, though he never spares Eli's weakness, leaves the impression "that with all his faults and imperfections he was still a servant of God." (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/4.htm)

**"He had judged Israel forty years."** This summary statement closes Eli's career. After the battle, the Philistines went on to destroy Shiloh itself (Ps 78:60-64; Jer 7:12; 26:9). (enduringword.com)

---

## vv. 19–20 — Phinehas' wife: labor, birth, and death

**Triple tragedy.** She heard in one moment of the ark's capture, her father-in-law's death, and her husband's death. The Hebrew says her labor pains "turned against her" (or "were rolled upon her") — an idiom for sudden and overwhelming labor. The attending women tried to comfort her with the birth of a son, but "she did not answer, nor did she regard it" — her grief overwhelmed even maternal joy. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/4.htm; enduringword.com)

---

## vv. 21–22 — "Ichabod … The glory has departed from Israel"

**The meaning of Ichabod.** Ellicott discusses three interpretations:
1. **"No glory"** — taking "I" as a simple negative: "not-glory" (the traditional reading)
2. **"Where is the glory?"** — taking "I" as an interrogative (rendered in the KJV margin)
3. **"Alas! the glory"** — taking "I" as an exclamation of bitter sorrow (Ellicott's preferred reading)

The Cambridge Bible notes that the narrator inserts the explanation parenthetically in v. 21, then repeats it in v. 22 — not as "mere tautology" but with a narrower focus: v. 21 connects Ichabod to the triple loss (ark, father-in-law, husband), while v. 22 focuses solely on the ark. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/4.htm; biblehub.com/study/chapters/1_samuel/4.htm)

**The real departure of glory.** Enduring Word, quoting Ellison, makes a crucial theological point: "The glory of God had indeed departed, but not because the ark of God had been captured; the ark had been captured because the glory had already departed." The glory left when Israel stopped repenting and started superstitiously trusting in the ark itself. (enduringword.com)

**God's sovereignty in the disaster.** Matthew Poole (cited in Enduring Word): "Thus as God was no loser by this event, so the Philistines were no gainers by it; and Israel, all things considered, received more good than hurt by it." (enduringword.com)

## Distinctive Protestant Traditions

### Reformed / Presbyterian

**Ligonier Ministries** (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/glory-departs-from-israel) emphasizes that when Scripture says God "departed," it does not mean He ceased to be omnipresent. Rather, "He has taken His blessing from them, that He is no longer protecting the visible covenant people from harm." God never abandons the invisible church (true believers), but He will reject the visible church when it declines into error. The loss of the ark was a sign that the Lord had left Israel "to fend for themselves."

**Albert Barnes** (Presbyterian, at studylight.org) focuses on Ichabod meaning "where is the glory?" and treats the departure of glory as the removal of the visible pledge of God's covenant presence.

### Baptist

**John Gill** (Baptist / Calvinist) sees the capture of the ark as an emblem "of Christ being delivered into the hands of the Gentiles, and of the Gospel being translated from the Jews to them." He draws a spiritual application: "so when the word, worship, and ordinances of God are removed from a people, the glory is gone from them." Gill treats Israel's trust in the ark as a warning against trusting in "carnal descent … rituals … ordinances … or any works of righteousness" instead of Christ alone. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/4.htm)

**Spurgeon** (Baptist, at studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/1-samuel-4.html) in his sermon "Ichabod" stressed that Israel "failed to perceive that sin was the secret of defeat" — sin on the part of Eli's sons, Eli himself, and the nation. He applies this to the church: when sin is tolerated, glory departs.

### Methodist / Wesleyan

**Joseph Benson** (Methodist, at studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/1-samuel-4.html) interprets Ichabod as "Where is the glory?" and notes that the ark is "often called God's glory." He emphasizes the piety of Phinehas' wife: "the public loss lay heavier upon her spirit than her personal and domestic calamity."

### Pentecostal / Charismatic

**David Guzik / Enduring Word** (enduringword.com) sees the chapter as a lesson about not treating God like a "good-luck charm" or a "genie." He stresses that God cannot be manipulated and that "loud worship proves nothing about the condition of the heart." The application is that "when we find ourselves defeated or struggling, we must be careful not to substitute religious activity … for genuine repentance and trust in God."

### Lutheran

No distinctively Lutheran commentary was found among the accessible sites (lcms.org and 1517.org did not yield results for this specific chapter).

## Other Views

### Jewish tradition (noted in Gill and Ellicott)

- The messenger from Benjamin was Saul (unfounded rabbinic tradition)
- Hophni and Phinehas stood fast by the ark, choosing death rather than surrender (Josephus, Antiquities 5.11.2)
- Eli charged his sons that if the ark were taken, they should not desire life (Josephus)

### Roman Catholic / Orthodox

The search of newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org did not yield specific verse-by-verse commentary on 1 Samuel 4 within the accessible results.

### Modern Scholarship

## Summary of Key Theological Themes Across Traditions

1. **God cannot be manipulated** — Israel's superstitious use of the ark was a form of pagan thinking imported into Yahwism. All traditions agree on this.

2. **Judgment on Eli's house** was both predicted (1 Sam 2:34) and fulfilled precisely.

3. **The ark ≠ God** — God is not bound to any physical object, however sacred. The capture of the ark proved this.

4. **Glory departs before the symbol departs** — The real departure happened when Israel abandoned genuine faith, not when the Philistines seized the ark.

5. **God's sovereignty in disaster** — What looked like total catastrophe was actually God beginning to show His glory, as the next chapters (1 Sam 5–6) demonstrate when the ark proves more powerful among the Philistines than it had been among the Israelites.
